summary: In Greek mythology, Ganymede or Ganymedes (Ancient Greek Γανυμήδης) is a Trojan divine hero, the most handsome of mortals, whom the gods carried off to Olympus to serve as Zeus's cup-bearer. Homer's Iliad already tells the abduction and Zeus's gift of immortal horses to Ganymede's father Tros; later tradition makes the relationship erotic and identifies the youth with the constellation Aquarius beside the eagle Aquila. The Latin form Catamitus gave English "catamite."
etymology: Xenophon's Socrates derives Ganymede from γάνυται ("he is glad") and μήδεα ("plans, counsel"), reading the name as joy in mind or thought; because μήδεα can also mean male genitals, some modern readers note a double entendre. The Latin Catamitus is a form of the same name.

sections.heading: Family
paragraphs: Ganymede is most often the son of Tros of Dardania — eponym of Troy — by Callirrhoe daughter of Scamander, or by Acallaris daughter of Eumedes. Brothers variously include Ilus, Assaracus, and Cleopatra or Cleomestra. Some authors instead make him son of Laomedon or of Ilus; rarer genealogies conflate him with other Dardanian names. Dictys Cretensis offers a non-Olympian variant in which Cretans abduct him.

sections.heading: Mythology
paragraphs: The Iliad describes Ganymede as loveliest of mortals, caught away by the gods to be Zeus's wine-pourer for the sake of his beauty; the Homeric Hymn to Aphrodite likewise has Zeus alone perform the abduction, without an explicit erotic frame. From Theognis onward the passion is often sexual. Later sources set the scene on Mount Ida: the youth tends sheep when an eagle — Zeus's bird, or Zeus himself — carries him to Olympus.

Zeus grants him eternal youth and immortality as cup-bearer, in place of or beside Hebe; Hera in the Aeneid and elsewhere regards him as a rival. Catasterism traditions identify him with Aquarius next to Aquila; Jupiter's largest moon was named Ganymede by Simon Marius in recognition of the myth. In compensation Zeus gave Tros horses that run over water and standing grain, delivered by Hermes.

Plato ties the pederastic reading to Crete; Athenaeus records a version in which Minos, not Zeus, takes the boy as cup-bearer. Xenophon's Socrates denies a sexual reading and stresses that Zeus granted Ganymede immortality for his soul. Apollonius shows him on Olympus furious at Eros for cheating at knucklebones; Virgil adds the pathos of tutors reaching in vain and hounds baying after their master's shadow.

sections.heading: Cult and symbolism
paragraphs: On Olympus Ganymede becomes the official cup-bearer; some accounts have Hebe relieved of that duty upon her marriage to Heracles, while the Iliad can still present Hebe (and once Hephaestus) pouring for the gods generally and Ganymede as Zeus's personal attendant. In poetry he became a standing symbol of the beautiful young male who attracts male desire — not always acquiescent.

Neoplatonic readers later treated the eagle-abduction as an allegory of the soul's ascent to spiritual perfection, a reading common in the Italian Renaissance alongside more frankly erotic treatments.

sections.heading: In the arts
paragraphs: Fifth-century Athenian vase-painters made the abduction a symposium favorite, often showing courtship gifts such as a cock. Leochares cast a celebrated bronze of Ganymede and the eagle, echoed in a Vatican marble group; Roman sarcophagi repeatedly show the eagle-lift as an image of ascent.

From the Renaissance through the Victorian era Ganymede was a major emblem of male–male desire in painting, sculpture, and drama — Correggio, Rubens, Rembrandt's bawling infant, Laviron at Versailles — before Antinous partly displaced him. Literary afterlives include Shakespeare's Rosalind-as-Ganymede in As You Like It, Marlowe's Dido, Goethe's "Ganymed" (set by Schubert and Wolf), and commercial appropriations such as Anheuser-Busch's eagle-and-youth imagery.
